title: Looking for the self
hookLine: an essay box that says 'tell us who you are'; Shantideva searches body and mind for the one who's typing
tomorrow: if no self is found, why be kind to anyone?

cards: The cursor has been blinking for twenty minutes. The box on the application says: tell us who you are. Version one: I'm a runner.
Delete; the knee ended that. Version two: I'm a big sister. True, but that's about her as much as me.
Version three: curious, kind, hardworking. It reads like anybody's. Every answer is real, and none of them is the thing itself.
Somewhere under all of it there must be someone, the one doing the typing. So where, exactly, is that one?

teach.h: ROOM BY ROOM: TEETH, HAIR, BONE.
teach.b: Shantideva asks the same question in chapter nine of his guide, and he searches the way you'd search a house for lost keys: room by room. The teeth, the hair, the nails: not the self. Bone, blood, sweat: not the self.
That's yesterday's body search again, but now he's after the owner. So he tries the mind. Is the self a feeling?
Feelings come and go all day; which one would it be? Is it a thought? Thoughts change faster than versions of an essay.
Awareness is always awareness of something, a sound, a screen. When the sound stops, where is the one who was hearing it? In every room he finds something.
He never finds a someone. Not found. Now the part that gets skipped.

teach.h: NOT FOUND IS NOT NOBODY HOME.
teach.b: Not found does not mean nobody's home. Remember the two truths: in everyday life there's a person with a name, a birthday and a sore knee, and Shantideva never denies her.
What he can't find is a fixed core, one thing that stays you underneath all the changing. The Pali word for this teaching is anatta, not-self. In Buddhist teaching, coming up empty here isn't a loss.
With no fixed self to defend, a bad version or a cruel comment has nothing permanent to stick to.
The writer at the keyboard is still there. Just lighter.

how: In Mahayana study, chapter nine of the Bodhicaryavatara is often read slowly with a teacher, and the search for the self is practiced as an analytical meditation: looking, not finding, and resting in that.

games.q: what does “looking for the self” mean?
o: searching body and mind for a fixed core, and not finding one
writing down your values until you know your true self
a long trip abroad to figure out what you want from life

games.q: the search, room by room — tap the pairs.
p: not the same as nobody home

s: in everyday life there's a person with a name. what isn't found is a fixed, unchanging core.
Shantideva searches the body part by part before he turns to the mind
teeth, hair, bone and blood first, then feelings, thoughts and awareness.
finding no self is meant to be a loss
in Buddhist teaching it's a loosening: nothing fixed to defend.

games.q: a classmate's comment, "you're so fake," has been stuck in your head all week. what does Shantideva's search suggest?
o: look for the fixed "you" it's stuck to. none turns up, so let it pass through.
work out who the real you is, then prove the comment wrong.
decide there's no you at all, so nothing anyone says can matter.
games.why: the search finds no fixed core for a label to stick to. it never says you don't matter: the person is still here, just lighter.

practice: Close your eyes and go looking, gently. Notice a sound, and ask whether the one hearing is in the ears. Notice a thought, and watch where it comes from and where it goes.
Each time you find something, a sensation, a memory, a plan, set it down softly and keep looking for the one who has it.

wordCard.voice: Looking for the self: Shantideva's search through body, feelings, thoughts and awareness for a fixed core that never turns up.

orig.note: Pali: not-self (Sanskrit anatman). The teaching that no fixed, unchanging core is found in body or mind.

carryVoice: Your line: not found. Someone is still here, with nothing fixed to defend. Forty-four days into the guide.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 9.57–9.69 (the search for the self: teeth, hair, nails, bone, blood are not the self; nor is consciousness)
